opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it played a pretty big role. When I was finishing up school, I was interested in doing something impactful, but I didn't have a clear picture of what that meant in practice. I'd been thinking a lot about global poverty and that general effective altruism set of questions, and I came across 80,000 Hours' materials around then. The framing of thinking about your career as your biggest lever for impact really stuck with me.

The AI piece was more gradual. I remember reading arguments that advanced AI could be one of the most consequential technologies we ever develop, and that relatively few people were working seriously on making it go well. At first I was somewhat skeptical. It felt speculative and far off. But the core argument kept nagging at me: if this technology really is transformative, and if the field is that neglected, then the value of having more careful, technically capable people working on it is enormous.

What I found most useful from 80,000 Hours wasn't necessarily being told "go work on AI safety." It was more the encouragement to build career capital and actually get good at something relevant, in my case machine learning engineering, rather than jumping straight into whatever felt most directly altruistic. That ended up mattering a lot. By the time I was seriously considering safety-focused work, I had real skills that were useful, and that made it possible to contribute meaningfully rather than just caring about the problem from the sidelines.

So I'd say it was less a single moment of persuasion and more a steady influence: it shaped how I thought about choosing problems, and it kept AI on my radar until the arguments, and frankly the pace of progress in the field, made it feel impossible to ignore.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a gradual influence and says 80,000 Hours encouraged him to build relevant career skills, but does not state that it urged him to move into AI safety sooner than he otherwise intended.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's actually kind of a funny story, because 80,000 Hours played a pretty direct role. I'd been thinking about effective altruism stuff for a while, and I think I came across the career guide early on, and the thing that stood out to me was just how seriously it took the question of, "What problem should you actually work on?" rather than just, "What job sounds fun?"

I remember reading the problem profiles, and AI was one of the areas they flagged as potentially really important and really neglected. And at the time I was somewhat skeptical, honestly. It seemed pretty speculative compared to things like global health, where you could see the impact much more concretely. But the argument that stuck with me was the one about how few people were actually working on it relative to how big the stakes could be. That asymmetry just kept nagging at me.

So I think I'd say 80,000 Hours did two things for me. One was giving me permission, in a sense, to take the idea seriously, because here was this group of people who'd thought hard about it and weren't crazy. And the second was more practical, which was helping me think through the actual path: what skills do you need, does it make sense to go do machine learning, is it better to be inside a lab or outside it. I actually talked to some people connected to 80,000 Hours during that period, and those conversations were useful for just getting a realistic picture of what the work would look like day to day.

I don't want to overstate it, I probably would have ended up somewhere in this space regardless, because a lot of my friends were drifting that way too. But I think it accelerated things by a few years, and it made the decision feel much more deliberate rather than something I just fell into.

r001.rationale: The candidate says 80,000 Hours played a direct role and accelerated his move toward the field by a few years, communicating that it prompted him to enter AI safety sooner than he otherwise would have.

astra-6.text: I think of 80,000 Hours’ role as helping me frame the decision: where could I use my skills to make the biggest difference? With AI safety, there’s both the question of how important the problem is and the question of whether I can contribute usefully. Those are separate questions, and taking both seriously is a helpful way to approach a career decision.

r001.rationale: The response says 80,000 Hours helped frame his career decision, but does not say they urged him to move into AI safety sooner than he otherwise intended.

sol-6.1.text: I think of 80,000 Hours as an important input, rather than the sole reason. It helped me take seriously the idea that my career could be a way to address very large problems, and that AI safety was worth considering in that context. But I’d be cautious about saying exactly what I would have done otherwise — career decisions have a lot of influences, and it’s hard to disentangle them.
